notes.title: Measuring a Turn — Key Metrics, Traces, Logs, Alerts
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Data hooks, OpenTelemetry traces, Agent Insights (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §7 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §10 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §11

TL;DR

Measure every turn, not every call. Five numbers tell you whether a voice agent is healthy: time to first audio, time to first token, tokens and cost, interruption rate, and fallback activation. Store them per turn with the turn id, trace each call end to end, log one line per decision, and alert on the one number users feel: end of speech to first audio at p95.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: turn endsper-turn metrics on the chat messagelog line + trace spandashboard per stagealert on p95

Recall

Prompt Answer
The five key metrics TTFA, TTFT, tokens and cost, interruption rate, fallback activation
Where LiveKit puts per-turn metrics each chat message's metrics (conversation_item_added)
The end-to-end field e2e_latency (assistant messages)
How to trace a call OpenTelemetry via set_tracer_provider, e.g. to Langfuse
The product-defining alert end of speech → first audio p95 > 800 ms
Draw one turn's metrics on its timeline end_of_turn_delay, llm_node_ttft, tts_node_ttfb, e2e_latency

The idea

Without it: "calls feel slow sometimes" with no way to say which stage, which vendor, which turn.

It does: puts a number on each stage of each turn, ties it to the decision that turn made, and keeps the call's whole story in one trace.

It costs: storage per turn, and care with what leaves the session: transcripts are personal data.

How it works

The five key metrics

Metric Means LiveKit field (Oct 2026) Ours Status
TTFA, time to first audio end of speech → first agent audio heard e2e_latency (per turn); tts_node_ttfb for the voice's share p50 3 383 ms, p95 4 948 ms; TTS TTFB p50 342 ms stored per turn
TTFT, time to first token reply request → first model token llm_node_ttft; LLMMetrics.ttft p50 442 ms, p95 1 714 ms stored per turn
Tokens and cost tokens per tier and model, cost per call session.usage; plugin metrics budget charged per call (600 calls, 1.5M tokens); cost per interview not measured budget / cost metric
Interruption rate barge-ins per agent turn, and the false ones InterruptionMetrics (adaptive mode); agent_false_interruption event logged per event; rate not aggregated log / metric
Fallback activation turns served by a backup vendor or a lower rung – (your code) voice-switch and PARSER … using … log lines; breaker state on the health API log / metric

"Time to first audio" means two different things; say which.

Name in use From → to What it tells you LiveKit field Ours (p50)
TTFA, end to end (voice-to-voice latency) the person's last word → first agent audio heard what the person feels; the product target ( p50 ≤ 450, p95 ≤ 800 ms) e2e_latency 3 383 ms ()
TTFA of the voice (TTS TTFB) first text sent to TTS → first audio byte back the voice vendor's share only tts_node_ttfb; TTSMetrics.ttfb 342 ms in calls, 314 ms warm in goldens ()
Playback latency audio ready → audio played (avatars, buffers) output-side delay playback_latency not tracked

End-to-end TTFA ≈ end_of_turn_delay + model llm_node_ttft + tts_node_ttfb + network and jitter, minus whatever overlapped. Our 3 383 ms is mostly the first term.

Also per turn: end_of_turn_delay (the biggest share), transcription_delay, whether the reply was interrupted. Per call: the exact config that ran (prompt version, plan, models, voice and feed, lexicon version, keyterm count, noise mode).

Layer Holds Ours
Per-turn store the metrics above, keyed by turn database rows
Logs one line per decision: USER … stt_delay= eou_delay=, AGENT … e2e= llm_ttft= tts_ttfb=, CHAIR, GATE, T1
Traces one session per call; LiveKit turn spans (agent_turn, …) and every graph run Langfuse via OpenTelemetry
Dashboards and alerts stage percentiles, rates Prometheus + Grafana
Vendor-side LiveKit Cloud Agent Insights: transcripts, traces, logs, recordings available, not used

Designed alerts: end of speech → first audio p95 > 800 ms (the product feels broken) · speculative hit rate < 0.70 (silently degraded into a questionnaire) · event-loop lag p99 > 50 ms (dead air coming).

Knobs

Knob Trade
allow_pii=False on the tracer strips conversation content before export; less to debug with
Trace sampling cost vs coverage; keep every turn's metrics even if traces are sampled
Percentiles per stage p50 for tuning, p95 for alerts

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Per-turn metrics stored e2e, TTFT, TTFB, transcription and end-of-turn delays, interrupted as_built §7
Per-call config stored prompt version, plan, STT, models, voice and feed, guard, lexicon, keyterms, noise mode as_built §7
Traces Langfuse, one session per interview as_built §7
Metrics export and alerts Prometheus, p95 > 800 ms alert and the others as_built §7 Enterprise, design §11

Measure it

  • Metric — the five above at p50 and p95, per stage, per vendor, per region.
  • See it — the interview page (transcript, per-turn latency, insights); Langfuse sessions; the agent log.
  • Bounded by — the alerts; the degradation ladder acts on the same signals.

Pitfalls

Measuring per call instead of per turn

  • Why it's tempting: calls are what you bill and count.
  • Why it's wrong: averages over a call hide the three slow turns people remember.
  • Think instead: store every turn with its stage breakdown; aggregate later.

Logging transcripts into every tool

  • Why it's tempting: debugging is easier with the words.
  • Why it's wrong: transcripts are personal data and now live in every vendor's logs.
  • Think instead: keep content in the session store, export metrics and IDs, use allow_pii=False where content isn't needed.

Watching TTFT and TTFB but not the end-of-turn wait

  • Why it's tempting: those are the vendor numbers.
  • Why it's wrong: in our calls the end-of-turn wait is ~2 s of a 3.4 s turn.
  • Think instead: end_of_turn_delay is the first panel on the dashboard.

Connections

… → observe — the numbers every other note quotes.

  • feeds the latency budget and the optimization playbook.
  • watches fallback activation.
  • is how evaluations are read in production.
  • Say it: Q31 · Q49

notes.title: Latency Optimization Playbook — The Levers, in Order
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §1 · LiveKit — Turn-taking tuning

TL;DR

Measure each stage's share of the turn first, then pull the lever with the biggest share. In our build the end-of-turn wait and one hot-path model call are the whole gap from 450 ms to 3.4 s; transport and the voice are close to budget. Change one lever per run and re-measure.

Stage: capture → … → endpoint → think → speak → … → observe · design time

Flow: per-turn metricsbiggest shareone leversame harnesscompare p50 and p95keep or revert

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four baseline rules stream everything, overlap STT → LLM → TTS, no blocking I/O, tight prompts
The two lines that hold our gap end-of-turn wait (~2 s) and the hot-path model call (~0.45 s)
The only lever worth more than a second tuning the end-of-turn wait
How to remove the model line pre-generate during speech
Why region placement matters here from India the model's median is the network
Draw the levers as a ranked bar chart of possible savings endpoint, speculation, region, second provider, then the rest

The idea

Without it: teams tune whatever is easiest (a faster model, a smaller chunk) while the biggest line sits untouched.

It does: ranks levers by measured share and expected saving, so the first change is the one that matters.

It costs: a measurement before every change, and the patience to change one thing at a time.

How it works

First, the four baseline rules (from a talk slide shared 16 Oct 2026). They make every stage cheap; the ranked levers below then remove what's left.

Rule What it means in a voice turn Owner note Ours
Stream everything audio in frames, interim transcripts, model tokens, TTS chunks: each stage emits its first piece as soon as it exists one turn, end to end STT interims on, model streamed, TTS one stream per segment
Parallelize STT → LLM → TTS overlap the stages instead of running them in series: start the model on the final phrase, synthesise sentence 2 while sentence 1 plays, analyse while the person still speaks preemptive generation, chunking, tiers all three on; full speculation not built
Avoid blocking I/O nothing synchronous on the call's event loop: no sync SDKs, no cold TLS mid-call, CPU work in a pool event-loop discipline warm pools, one process per call; loop-lag metric not built
Keep prompts tight fewer input tokens means less prefill before the first token; short outputs mean less to generate and say model on the hot path, writing for the ear persona prompt 148 words, last 8 messages kept verbatim (RECENT_TURNS), reply cap 600 tokens (reasoning model)

Then the levers, ranked by what they would save here:

Rank Lever Stage Expected saving Cost Status
1 Tune the end-of-turn wait on recorded answers (max_delay 3.5 → ~2.0 s touches 39% of turns) endpoint > 1 s: trial cut mean wait 2.68 → 2.24 s, median e2e 4.19 → 3.74 s cut-offs; split answers trial, not adopted
2 Find why short turns wait for their final transcript (23% of turns) transcribe up to ~0.9 s average overrun investigation first
3 Speculative pre-generation: no model call after the turn think ~0.45 s p50, ~1.7 s p95 wasted drafts, harder state
4 Region: media, STT, voice and model near the caller carry, think ~75 ms per round trip (90 vs 15 ms, design §3) plus the model's network share a region to run
5 Second model provider via a router think the vendor's tail (p95 1.7 s) stops being ours a second set of goldens
6 Preemptive generation think TTFT on turns that commit unchanged wasted calls on
7 Sentence chunking with a 12-word flush speak ~240 ms on long sentences choppier joins on
8 Warm connections, prewarmed models speak, detect ~620 ms cold connect on turn one idle resources on
9 Faster TTS voice or vendor speak ~40–80 ms to reach the 300 ms gate voice quality, lexicon (Cartesia to explore)

Knobs

The levers above are the knobs; each note owns its own: endpointing · speculation · hot-path model · chunking.

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Gap p50 3 383 ms vs 450 ms target as_built §3
Lever order as ranked above (as_built's four, plus the late-transcript finding) as_built §3, FLOW §1

Measure it

  • Metric — e2e_latency p50/p95 before and after, and the stage the lever targets.
  • See it — the synthetic caller (tests/live_voice.py) for endpoint changes; per-turn metrics on real calls.
  • Bounded by — revert if p95 or the cut-off rate gets worse.

Pitfalls

Optimising the visible vendor number

  • Why it's tempting: TTFT and TTFB are on every vendor's page.
  • Why it's wrong: together they're ~0.8 s of our 3.4 s; the wait is the rest.
  • Think instead: sort the stages by measured share and start at the top.

Changing several levers at once

  • Why it's tempting: faster progress.
  • Why it's wrong: if p95 moves, you don't know which change did it, or which one hurt cut-offs.
  • Think instead: one change per run, same audio, same harness.

Connections

… → observe — what to change once the numbers are in.

  • ranks the lines of the latency budget.
  • reads per-turn metrics.
  • Say it: Q4 · Q51

notes.title: Evaluating a Voice Agent — Goldens, Test Conditions, Simulations
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/transcript_quality.md §7 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/goldens/ (stt_tts, intent, t1, scoring, voice_interview_cases.md) · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/tests/live_voice.py · LiveKit — Agent Simulations, Unit tests

TL;DR

Test a voice agent in four layers, from cheap to real: component goldens (STT, TTS, each model's job), scripted conversations (text, no audio), synthetic callers (generated speech played into a real room), and human calls (real voices, rooms, mics). For each layer, list the conditions that break voice agents (noise, other voices, accents, code-switching, pauses, short turns, interruptions, echo, bad networks) and gate only what the product claims.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: component goldensscripted conversationssynthetic caller in a roomhuman callsgate on claimed conditionschange one thing, re-run

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four layers component goldens, scripted conversations, synthetic callers, human calls
What synthetic audio can't tell you real accents, laptop mics, rooms, the way people pause
What to gate only the conditions the product claims to support; report the rest
The rule when tuning one change per run, same harness, same audio
What a scripted voice case needs what to say, what must happen, where to see it, pass criterion
Draw the test-conditions matrix rows: conditions; columns: layer; cells: tested / not tested

The idea

Without it: every change is judged by one engineer's demo call, in one quiet room, in one accent.

It does: fixes the inputs (sentences, audio, scripted turns, conditions) so a change shows up as a number, and names the conditions where voice agents fail so they're tested on purpose.

It costs: recordings of real people and real rooms, which are slow to collect and the most valuable part.

How it works

The four layers

Layer Runs Catches Ours
1. Component goldens each stage alone on fixed inputs vocabulary, pronunciation, TTFB, intent labels, scoring drift goldens/stt_tts, intent (37 cases), t1, scoring
2. Scripted conversations the brain on text turns, no audio move selection, budgets, idempotent re-runs unit tests (test_chair.py, test_gate.py, test_echo.py) ; LiveKit offers unit tests and scenario simulations
3. Synthetic caller generated speech played as a mic into a real room endpointing, cut-offs, barge-in, echo tests/live_voice.py (10 turns, cached audio), --echo
4. Human calls a person, a laptop, a room everything synthetic hides voice_interview_cases.md: 30+ scripted cases (V-01 … V-59) ; results log still empty

The test-conditions matrix (what breaks voice agents, and what we have tested)

Condition What it breaks Tested how Result Status
Steady noise (fan, AC) VAD false starts, recognition brown noise + 100 Hz hum mixed in at 15, 10, 5 dB SNR ≤ 3–4 points of term recall lost at 5 dB: noise is not the main loss synthetic
Background voices (TV, people) second-voice false alarms, noise filter removing the speaker live call with Krisp bvc bvc removed a quiet laptop mic entirely (26 Sep 2026); nc is now the default one live call
Accent (Indian English) recognition, fairness synthetic Indian-accent voice through prod config recall 96%, WER 11.2% synthetic only
Code-switching (Hinglish) empty or mixed-script transcripts 1 code-switch sentence in 20 STT goldens; en-IN vs multi 50% recall; multi cost 10 points of term recall thin
Domain vocabulary misheard terms 10 tech-vocab items, out-of-list, homophone traps 99% / 50% / 100%
Numbers wrong figures 3 number items, variants accepted 95% recall
Long thinking pauses cut-offs live caller: 1.5 s and 2.6 s silences mid-sentence cut-offs at the 0.8 s floor ("The main trade-off was, um,") synthetic caller
Short complete turns dead air "Are you there?", "Three questions." held to the 3.5 s ceiling; late finals on short turns live log
Fragments early commit "So the thing is that", then silence "with the" committed at 0.8 s in logs live log
Backchannels over the agent false barge-in V-23 vad mode stops on "mm-hm" by design case written, not logged
Noise over the agent false barge-in V-21 resume after 2 s case written, not logged
Echo (speakers, no headphones) the agent's words scored as the person's live_voice --echo: her own question played back dropped twice, re-asked 13 Oct 2026
Asking for time, off-topic, abuse, injection wrong moves intent goldens; V-54 … V-59; V-30 rules 2/37 vs model 36–37/37 non-answers
Network drop, muted mic, autoplay blocked stuck calls V-40 … V-42 – case written, not logged
Phone audio (8 kHz) recognition – – not tested
Long call (45 min), many turns budgets, memory, drift – – not tested
Concurrency (vendor queues) TTFB and TTFT tails – – not tested (degradation)

Knobs

Knob Our value Trade
Audio source recorded if present, else 3 synthetic voices realism vs effort; recordings/ is still empty
Gated categories tech vocab, numbers, Indian context, homophones gating code-switch would hide it
Synthetic caller 10 cached utterances with timed pauses repeatable; cleaner and more evenly paced than people
Scenario simulation (LiveKit) not used LLM-driven callers in CI vs real audio

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Component goldens STT 20 items in 6 categories, TTS lexicon and TTFB, intent 37, T1, scoring goldens/
Gates term recall ≥ 90%, WER ≤ 15%, lexicon ≥ 85%, TTFB ≤ 300 ms goldens §3; TTFB fails on every voice
Synthetic caller used for the max_delay trial and the echo fix FLOW §1, §2
Human recordings none goldens §3: "the single most valuable next step"
Manual voice cases written, results table empty voice_interview_cases.md

Measure it

  • Metric — pass rate per layer and per condition; trend per release; one number per condition the product claims.
  • See it — goldens/*/reports/; per-turn e2e, eou_delay, cut-off lines from the live caller; Langfuse sessions for human calls.
  • Bounded by — a gate that fails the release, and the rule of one change per run.

Pitfalls

Calling synthetic goldens "accuracy"

  • Why it's tempting: they are cheap, repeatable and look good.
  • Why it's wrong: clean synthetic voices overstate accuracy and pace pauses evenly; the conditions that break agents aren't in them.
  • Think instead: synthetic as the regression line; human recordings per condition as the truth.

Testing the happy path only

  • Why it's tempting: a full interview that works feels like proof.
  • Why it's wrong: failures live in the conditions: fans, TV in the background, a two-second pause, "mm-hm", speakers instead of headphones.
  • Think instead: the conditions matrix, with a row for each, and "not tested" written where it's true.

Writing manual cases and never logging them

  • Why it's tempting: writing the case feels like testing it.
  • Why it's wrong: an empty results table means nobody knows which cases pass today.
  • Think instead: run the cases before each release and record pass, fail and e2e per case.

Connections

… → observe — how every stage is judged.

  • includes recognition goldens, the lexicon round trip and voice gates.
  • tunes endpointing and barge-in.
  • checks the failure paths of the degradation ladder.
  • Say it: Q19 · Q49

notes.title: The Degradation Ladder — Fallbacks, Circuit Breakers, the LLM Gateway
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §2.5, §8 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §9 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/resilience.py, brain/llms.py · LiveKit — Fallback strategies · LiteLLM — Router

TL;DR

A live call can't show an error page. Every dependency gets a next rung: a circuit breaker that fails fast, a second provider, a cheaper behaviour, and finally a scripted floor that still finishes the conversation. Media recovery is the transport's job; what the conversation does when something degrades is yours.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: call failsopen: skip the dead vendornext providernext behaviourscripted floorthe call still completes

Recall

Prompt Answer
Breaker states closed → open (fail fast) → half-open (one trial) → closed or open
Why a breaker, not just retries without it every turn burns a full timeout on a vendor known to be down
What an LLM gateway adds one place for provider fallbacks, retries, routing and spend, per model
The floor scripted mode: a fixed plan, no adaptation, still a valid transcript
The worst outcome to design against silence with a person waiting
Draw the ladder for the reply model primary → breaker open → second provider → planned question → bridge line

The idea

Without it: a vendor's bad minute is the product's bad minute: retries pile up, every turn waits out a timeout, and the call goes silent.

It does: decides in advance, per dependency, what happens at each level of failure, so degradation is graceful and visible in logs.

It costs: a second vendor per stage (cost, a second set of goldens), breaker thresholds to tune (too tight flaps, too loose hammers), and a weaker experience on the lower rungs.

How it works

Per dependency (our design, ADD §8 and design §9)

Dependency Rung 1 Rung 2 Floor Built?
Reply model retry 1 second provider via the LLM router planned question word for word, bridge line retry + breaker; router
Background models (T1) deadline backup provider shed T1 (Assessor first), rule-based picker rule fallback
Parser models Cerebras primary OpenAI fallback (WithFallback) error
TTS retry 1 OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts (FallbackAdapter) text on screen voice; text
STT repeat request second STT vendor text input in the session
Media LiveKit reconnects, ICE restart bridge line over the gap flush turns, queue scoring, offer resume LiveKit; rest
Redis checkpoint log and continue – – (checkpoint only, never on the turn path)

The LLM gateway (router). One in-process router (LiteLLM in the design) sits in front of every model call: a list of providers per model, retries, fallbacks on 429 / timeout / 5xx, and a per-vendor breaker, with no network hop. It turns "add a second provider" from a code change in every caller into a config line. LiveKit has the same idea per stage as fallback adapters (FallbackAdapter for TTS, STT and LLM).

Knobs

Knob Our value Raise it → Lower it →
Breaker threshold 5 consecutive upstream failures fewer false opens, more wasted calls opens on blips, shunts to weaker models
Cooldown 20 s, doubling to 300 s longer on the fallback retries a dead vendor sooner
Hot-path retries 1 survives blips, longer wait faster to the fallback
Breaker scope per vendor, per process – global state: coordination cost

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Circuit breakers every model, named; closed → open after 5 → half-open after 20 s, cooldown doubling to 300 s resilience.py
Reply model Cerebras gpt-oss-120b, 1 retry, breaker speaker; no second provider brain/llms.py
LLM router with fallbacks LiteLLM, in-process; "replaces this later" llms.py docstring; ADD §8.3; as_built §3 lever 4
Parser fallback chain Cerebras → OpenAI, logged WithFallback
TTS fallback Deepgram → OpenAI after 1 retry, logged main.py
Budgets 600 calls / 1.5M tokens per interview; T1 300; guard 240 as_built §4
Silence watchdog 4 s → bridge line, 10 s → close (design); built: 10 / +25 / +25 s check-ins / ADD §8.2; silence
Text fallback type the rest of the interview, modality = text_fallback on the scorecard design §9

Measure it

  • Metric — breaker opens per vendor per day, share of turns served on each rung, calls completed in degraded mode.
  • See it — breaker snapshots (resilience.breakers()), PARSER … failed, using … and voice-switch log lines.
  • Bounded by — the scripted floor and per-interview budgets: the call completes even with every model down.

Pitfalls

Retries as the fallback

  • Why it's tempting: most failures are blips.
  • Why it's wrong: against a vendor that is down, each retry is another full timeout of silence, on every turn.
  • Think instead: a breaker that fails fast, and a different provider or behaviour behind it.

A second provider nobody has measured

  • Why it's tempting: any model is better than none.
  • Why it's wrong: a fallback with worse TTFT, a different voice or worse vocabulary changes the call in ways nobody tested.
  • Think instead: run the same goldens on every rung; log every switch.

Failing the call when a dependency fails

  • Why it's tempting: an error is honest.
  • Why it's wrong: the person is mid-conversation; a planned question or a typed answer finishes the job.
  • Think instead: design the floor first (scripted mode), then the rungs above it.

Connections

… → observe — what happens when any stage fails.

  • catches the hot-path model and the voice.
  • ends in the same ladder as speculative pre-generation: planned question, bridge line.
  • tested by evaluating a voice agent.
  • general pattern in reliability engineering (agentic).
  • Say it: Q46 · Q45

notes.title: Scaling to 1,000 Concurrent Calls — Vendors Are the Ceiling
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/scaling_1k.md · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_capacity.md Part B · LiveKit — Server options

TL;DR

Split the system into tiers that scale on different signals: control plane on requests, media on tracks, agents on concurrent calls, after-call work on queue depth. Nodes are the cheap, boring part. The ceiling at 1,000 calls is vendor concurrency and cost: 1,000 open STT, TTS and model streams at once, and first-byte times that climb when a vendor queues you.

Stage: capture → carry → … → observe · design time

Flow: calls ↑agent processes ↑ (1 per call)SFU tracks ↑ (2 per call)vendor streams ↑ (3 per call)first vendor limit hitTTFB / TTFT climb

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four tiers and their scaling signals control plane: requests · SFU: tracks · agents: concurrent calls · after-call: queue depth
Agent processes at 1,000 calls 1,000 (one per call)
SFU tracks at 1,000 calls ~2,000; multi-node with Redis needed
Bottleneck order vendor concurrency + cost → SFU topology → loop lag → node CPU/RAM
What to load-test first calls per pod (everything else scales from it)
Draw the four tiers with their autoscalers HPA on CPU, nodes on tracks, HPA on jobs, KEDA on queue

The idea

Without it: the plan starts with node maths, the cluster can host 1,000 calls, and the TTS vendor serialises at 200 streams.

It does: scales each tier on its own signal and plans vendor contracts before the cluster.

It costs: four deployables and a load test that must use real vendors.

How it works

500 calls 1,000 calls
Agent processes 500 1,000
vCPU / RAM used (0.5 vCPU, 0.5 GB per call) ~250 / ~250 GB ~500 / ~500 GB
Session pods (8 per pod) ~63 ~125
On-demand nodes (16 vCPU, with headroom) ~27 ~42–55
SFU audio tracks ~1,000 ~2,000 (~80 Mbps; CPU and connections are the limit)
Vendor streams (STT, TTS, model) 500 each 1,000 each: the real ceiling
Control-plane replicas 3–6 3–6
After-call workers (~4 min/job, batch in ~30 min) ~67 ~134, spot, scale to zero

All planning numbers, gated on a load test. Controls: LiveKit load_threshold (0.7 CPU default) and idle processes per server, HPA on concurrent jobs, a cluster autoscaler, circuit breakers so a throttled vendor fails fast instead of 1,000 calls waiting out a timeout.

Knobs

Knob Trade
Calls per pod density vs CPU-starved turns
Node type on-demand for live media and agents (never spot); spot for after-call work
Vendor contracts dedicated capacity vs shared queues
Admission control refuse new calls near a vendor limit vs degrade live ones

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Scale plan as above scaling_1k, capacity Part B
Calls per pod open question C.1, not load-tested scaling_1k §2.3
Vendor TTFB under concurrency unmeasured; at 450 ms the 800 ms target fails on arithmetic decision_rationale weak point 2
Today LiveKit Cloud, prototype traffic as_built

Measure it

  • Metric — p95 TTFB and TTFT as concurrency rises; vendor 429s; CPU per call; SFU CPU per track.
  • See it — a load test with synthetic callers through real vendors, stepping 50 → 500 → 1,000.
  • Bounded by — breakers, admission control, and on-demand nodes for anything live.

Pitfalls

Planning scale from node maths

  • Why it's tempting: CPU per call is easy to measure.
  • Why it's wrong: nodes are linear and cheap; vendor queues are not.
  • Think instead: get vendor concurrency limits in writing first, then size the cluster.

Load-testing with mocked vendors

  • Why it's tempting: cheap and repeatable.
  • Why it's wrong: the thing that breaks is the vendor's first byte under load.
  • Think instead: at least one run through real vendors at target concurrency.

Connections

… → observe — what changes when there are many calls.

  • scales agent processes and the four tiers.
  • protected by breakers and fallbacks.
  • Say it: Q15 · Q47

notes.title: Cost per Minute — What a Voice Call Spends
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/scaling_1k.md §3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §4 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §10 (utkarsh_cost_per_session_inr)

TL;DR

A voice minute pays for five things at once: STT minutes, model tokens (including drafts that were thrown away), TTS characters, media (SFU minutes, TURN relay) and compute for the agent process. Price each per minute from the vendors' own pages on the day you plan, measure the real usage per call, and watch the hidden multipliers: preemptive re-drafts, background analysis, after-call scoring.

Stage: capture → … → observe · design time

Flow: per call: STT min + tokens (hot + background + after-call) + TTS chars + media min + agent CPU÷ call minutescost per minute per tenant

Recall

Prompt Answer
The five cost lines STT, model tokens, TTS, media, compute
The hidden multipliers preemptive re-drafts, background (T1) calls, after-call scoring
Usually the biggest at scale vendor usage (STT, TTS, tokens), not nodes
Our cost per interview not measured
Draw a stacked bar per minute five segments; mark which scale with talk time vs turns

The idea

Without it: a budget per call that counts model calls but not what they cost, and a surprise invoice at 1,000 calls.

It does: turns usage per call into money per minute, per tenant, and makes each architectural choice show up as a line.

It costs: keeping vendor prices current; they change often.

How it works

Line Scales with Our usage meter Watch
STT candidate talk time audio minutes interims don't cost extra minutes
Model tokens turns × (hot path + background + guard), plus after-call tokens per tier and model re-drafts and T1 restarts multiply tokens
TTS characters spoken characters re-said replies after echo
Media call minutes × participants; TURN relay for ~10–25% of clients SFU minutes relay bandwidth
Compute concurrent calls (0.5 vCPU, 0.5 GB per call, planned) pod hours idle prewarmed processes

Prices are volatile: read them from each vendor's pricing page and date them; don't copy numbers into notes.

Knobs

Knob Lowers cost by Costs
Preemptive generation off fewer wasted drafts latency
Smaller background models, debounce fewer T1 tokens weaker insights
Batch after-call scoring, cache rubric prefixes cheaper T2 –
Dedicated vendor capacity lower unit price at volume commitment

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Budgets 600 calls, 1.5M tokens per interview; T1 300 calls; guard 240 as_built §4
Cost model per tenant STT minutes, voice characters, tokens by tier as_built §4 Enterprise
Cost per interview not measured as_built §4
Ceiling vendor concurrency + cost first scaling_1k §3

Measure it

  • Metric — cost per call minute, per tenant, split by line; tokens per turn by tier.
  • See it — usage on each vendor's dashboard against our per-call counters.
  • Bounded by — per-interview budgets and a fixed closing line when they run out.

Pitfalls

Budgeting only the hot-path model

  • Why it's tempting: it's the call you think about.
  • Why it's wrong: background analysis, guards, re-drafts and after-call scoring can outspend it.
  • Think instead: meter tokens per tier from day one.

Connections

… → observe — the money side of every design choice.

  • driven by preemptive generation and the tiers.
  • the first bottleneck in scaling.
  • Say it: Q18

notes.title: Recording, Transcripts and PII
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Record audio and video, PII redaction (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §8

TL;DR

A voice call produces three kinds of personal data: audio, transcripts, and telemetry that may contain both. Record only with consent captured first, keep what you need for the product's purpose, redact what leaves the session store, and delete on a schedule.

Stage: capture → … → observe · per session

Flow: consentrecord or nottranscript kept for feedbackredact before exportretention job deletes

Recall

Prompt Answer
Three kinds of voice data audio, transcripts, telemetry
Consent rule captured before any recording starts
LiveKit Cloud's PII redaction after the session, during upload; 41 categories, 36 on by default; English-only, best effort, fails closed
Redacted audio sounds like a beep over the segment
Strip content from traces allow_pii=False on the tracer
Draw where each kind of data goes and who can read it session store, traces, vendor logs, recordings

The idea

Without it: recordings exist that people weren't told about, and transcripts sit in every vendor's logs.

It does: decides per data kind whether it's kept, where, for how long, and in what form.

It costs: less data for debugging, and a consent step in the flow.

How it works

Path (LiveKit, Oct 2026) What it gives
LiveKit Cloud session recording audio stored automatically, with noise cancellation and PII redaction if enabled; playback in Agent Insights
Egress (room composite, tracks) your own storage, more control, video
PII redaction transcripts, dashboard transcript, audio (beep), telemetry; record: { redaction: true } per session; SDK ≥ 1.8.0
Tracer allow_pii=False strips conversation content before export

Knobs

Knob Trade
Record audio debugging and audit vs consent and storage
Retention period evidence vs exposure
Redaction before export safety vs debug detail

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Session recording off: candidates weren't told, so nothing is recorded as_built §8
Transcript kept to prepare feedback as_built §8
Storage Postgres with row-level security; graph checkpoints local and dropped after the call; retention job removes sessions as_built §8
Target consent before recording; residency by region; PII removed from anything that leaves the store as_built §8 Enterprise

Measure it

  • Metric — share of sessions with consent recorded; data past retention (should be zero).
  • See it — retention job logs; what your trace backend actually stores.
  • Bounded by — retention, row-level security, redaction on export.

Pitfalls

Turning on recording because the platform makes it one switch

  • Why it's tempting: it helps debugging.
  • Why it's wrong: without consent it's a legal and trust problem, and it's the person's voice.
  • Think instead: consent first, purpose stated, retention set.

Connections

… → observe — what is kept.

  • traces governed in measuring a turn.
  • consent is one of the four production workflows in handoffs, tasks and workflows.
  • recordings would feed goldens, with consent.
  • Say it: Q24

notes.title: Fairness Across Accents — Per-Cohort Accuracy as a Release Gate
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §5.4, §11 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/decision_rationale.md weak point 3 · Indic speech at IISc

TL;DR

Recognition accuracy differs by accent, and in a judged conversation that difference turns into a score difference even if accent is never passed to the scorer: a speaker transcribed worse looks vaguer, and vagueness is penalised. Refusing to use accent isn't enough; you have to measure accuracy per cohort and treat a gap as a release blocker.

Stage: capture → … → transcribe → … → observe · design time

Flow: accentmore STT errorsanswer reads vaguerscorer marks it downunfair outcome, with no accent signal anywhere

Recall

Prompt Answer
How bias enters without an accent signal through transcription quality
Why "don't pass accent to the scorer" isn't enough the transcript already carries the difference
The measurement WER and term recall per accent cohort, plus score distributions per cohort
What STT confidence may be used for a repeat request only, never scoring
Other fairness stages turn-taking windows per accent, the persona's neutrality
Draw the bias path accent → STT errors → vaguer text → lower score

The idea

Without it: a fair-looking pipeline (no accent features) that systematically scores some speakers lower.

It does: makes the hidden path measurable and gates releases on it.

It costs: labelled recordings per cohort, with consent, and a fairness review of every model or vendor change.

How it works

Where unfairness can enter Check
STT accuracy WER and term recall per cohort
Endpointing cut-off rate per cohort (language-aware pause handling)
Language choice empty-transcript rate on code-switched speech (accent and language)
The agent's manner praise or judgement per candidate (persona)
Scores distributions and adverse-impact ratios per cohort

Knobs

Knob Trade
Gate threshold for cohort gaps strict: fewer releases; loose: fairness debt
Per-cohort tuning (endpoint windows, vocabulary) fairness vs one config

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Accent never reaches the scorer STT confidence used only for repeats design §5.4
Per-cohort STT metric specified; nothing measured decision_rationale weak point 3
Data synthetic Indian-accent voice only; no human recordings goldens

Measure it

  • Metric — WER, term recall, cut-off rate and mean score per cohort; the largest gap between cohorts.
  • See it — goldens split by cohort once recordings exist; production scores aggregated by cohort with consent.
  • Bounded by — a release gate on the largest gap.

Pitfalls

Calling the pipeline fair because accent isn't a feature

  • Why it's tempting: no protected attribute is used.
  • Why it's wrong: the transcript already encodes it as errors, and the scorer reads the transcript.
  • Think instead: measure outcomes per cohort; fairness is a number, not a design statement.

Connections

… → observe — fairness as a measured property.

  • starts at accent and language.
  • tested in evaluating a voice agent.
  • Say it: Q50

notes.title: Region Placement — Everything Near the Caller
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §3 lever 3

TL;DR

A turn makes several round trips (media to the SFU, audio to STT, a model call, text to TTS). Each one pays the distance. Put the media server, the agent and every vendor endpoint in the callers' region, or the network becomes the biggest model in the pipeline.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

The idea

Hop Regional Distant Note
Media round trip (design §3) ~15 ms ~90 ms 13% of a ~700 ms budget
Model first token from India – ~850 ms for every OpenAI model tried network-bound, not model-bound ()
TTS cold connect from India – ~620–700 ms on turn one then warm

🔊 In our system

Callers in India; LiveKit Cloud, Deepgram, Cerebras and OpenAI are all remote (as_built §3). Target: everything in the candidates' region, data residency by region.
